http://www.bignewsnetwork.com/news/27920.text: Big News Network.com Hungary's ex-PM demands restoration of democracy BUDAPEST, Hungary: Hungary's former nationalist prime minister Viktor Orbán, who lost power after 16 years in an election in April, has called on his supporters to restore democracy. He said that the new government has destroyed democracy in the country. Orbán made his first strong political comments since his heavy election defeat late on July 21 through a Facebook post. He issued what he called a "Statement of Resistance" shortly after his Fidesz party said that prosecutors had searched offices where its internet servers are located. Prosecutors told Reuters in an email that the action was connected to an investigation into suspected misuse of funds and other crimes at the National Culture Fund (NKA) during Orbán's time in government. Orbán said that Hungary is no longer a democratic state after the new center-right government led by Prime Minister Peter Magyar passed a constitutional amendment. According to Orbán, this amendment ended the terms of both the president and the head of the constitutional court. Magyar's Tisza party has denied accusations that it is acting in an authoritarian way toward political opponents. The party has promised to reduce corruption, which it says was widespread under Orbán's government, as part of its effort to bring Hungary back in line with the European Union. Orbán himself faced strong criticism during his time in power over democratic standards in Hungary. His government often clashed with the European Union on issues such as the rule of law and the rights of minorities. Orbán has denied all corruption allegations. He said that a period of tyranny had begun again in Hungary. He also said that the new political system created in this way is not legitimate, and that Fidesz will use all peaceful means, both inside and outside parliament, to oppose what he described as abuse of power. Magyar's Tisza party holds a large majority in parliament, which allows it to reverse changes introduced during Orbán's time in office that Magyar says weakened democracy. The constitutional amendment ended the term of President Tamás Sulyok, stating that there had been a serious loss of public trust in him. Sulyok had been elected in 2024 by lawmakers from Orbán's Fidesz party. Parliament is expected to elect a new president soon. Magyar's Tisza party currently enjoys strong public support. A poll by the polling company Median earlier in the month showed that 60 percent of voters support Tisza, compared to 18 percent for Fidesz. Since the election, Fidesz has faced internal problems, including the resignation of its parliamentary group leader last week. http://www.euronews.com/2026/08/24/houth.text: Yemen's Houthis said on Monday that their forces hit a Saudi oil tanker in the Red Sea with a ballistic missile, as the Iran-backed group continues to pursue a maritime blockade of the Bab el-Mandeb strait, another crucial artery for global shipping."The strike was accurate and direct, resulting in a fire breaking out aboard the vessel and causing a number of other ships that were present in the target area to flee," the Houthis said in a statement."This targeting comes as part of the implementation of the Armed Forces' decision to ban maritime navigation by the Saudi enemy."The Houthi claim came hours after a British maritime agency said a tanker struck by an "unknown projectile" caught fire off Saudi Arabia's Red Sea coast."The Company Security Officer reported a tanker has been struck by (an) unknown projectile causing a fire to the vessel on the main deck," said the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations."All crew are safe and accounted for and no environmental impact has been reported," it added.The incident took place 63 nautical miles west of the Saudi city of Yanbu, the agency reported. Yanbu lies hundreds of kilometres north of Yemen.British maritime security firm Vanguard Tech also said a Saudi-flagged vessel had been hit by a missile and caught fire.The Bab al-Mandeb strait, which connects the southern Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean, carries roughly 12% of global maritime trade.The Houthis disrupted it severely with their campaign against Israel-linked shipping during the Israel-Hamas war in Gaza, claiming it was in a show of support for Palestinians.The Bab el-Mandeb campaign comes at a time when the Strait of Hormuz, the Gulf's other critical chokepoint, remains under blockade after the US-Iran war continued following the collapse of the interim deal between the two sides.The Houthis have reportedly held talks with Tehran on instituting a toll for cargo ships passing through the strait akin to the one Iran is eyeing for Hormuz.Turning up the heatThe group — formally known as Ansar Allah — has been attacking Saudi Arabia's ships after declaring a maritime blockade of the country last month.Hostilities erupted in July after the group welcomed an Iranian plane in Yemen's capital Sana'a, setting off a spate of tit-for-tat attacks.The Houthis have hit Saudi tankers in the Red Sea and attacked Yemeni government forces since the latest round of fighting broke out.They have also repeatedly targeted Saudi Arabia's oil infrastructure and airports.Riyadh has since launched air strikes on Houthi military positions and infrastructure in Hodeidah, Yemen's main Red Sea port.The blockade has threatened Saudi Arabia's ability to export millions of barrels of crude oil per day.On 31 July, Riyadh announced a new multinational maritime defence coalition, with 14 countries, including Pakistan, Turkey and Egypt, signing a founding statement to protect Red Sea shipping.Embroiled in more than a decade of its own war, Yemen became the latest country to be dragged into the Iran war last month, when the Houthis upended a 2022 truce with the country's internationally recognised government.The Houthis, who came to power in late 2014 after storming Sana'a and seizing the presidential palace and key military sites, forcing Yemen's government into exile, are part of Tehran's so-called Axis of Resistance.The Axis is a loose network of militant groups in several countries in the region, including Hezbollah in Lebanon, Hamas in Gaza and militias in Iraq, which are all backed, trained and equipped by the IRGC to varying degrees.While the Houthis do not control the part of Yemen’s coastline along Bab el-Mandeb, they hold territory less than 100 kilometres away.

https://www.theguardian.com/theguardian/.text: IscoBusquet asks: The report into Russian political interference in the UK stated that the security services were not given permission to look into any interference in the Brexit referendum because of political sensitivity. Is it possible for them to revisit this? Luke: We never got to see the confidential annex attached to the Russia Report. (If someone has a copy, please send to me ℅ Guardian!) But yes, it revealed that none of the state agencies investigated Russian interference in the run-up to the 2016 referendum. Neither Labour nor the Conservatives are especially keen to examine what happened. We know the following: that the Kremlin backed Brexit, seeing it as a way of weakening the UK, politically and economically, and estranging it from its European partners. Russian trolls posted thousands of pro-Brexit messages, as well as inflammatory stories about immigrants. I suspect there was espionage too. We need to find out what happened in order to safeguard elections in future.
